results.title: Safety Monitoring and Adverse Event Reporting in Clinical Trials: Regulatory Requirements and Best Practices
results.content: # Safety Monitoring and Adverse Event Reporting in Clinical Trials: Regulatory Requirements and Best Practices. Clinical trials must include safety monitoring and adverse event reporting because they guarantee the health and safety of research participants. Depending on the nation and location, there are different regulatory criteria and best practices for safety monitoring and adverse event reporting, but they all typically work to ensure that clinical trials are run morally and safely. The ICH E6(R2) guideline on Good Clinical Practice (GCP) outlines the standards for safety monitoring, reporting, and management of adverse events. ⮚    Trial Protocol: The clinical trial protocol must include a section on safety monitoring and adverse event reporting. In conclusion, safety oversight and adverse event reporting are crucial aspects of clinical research. By following best practices and regulatory requirements, sponsors can ensure the security of clinical trial data and the well-being of research participants. https://paradigmit.com/safety-monitoring-and-adverse-event-reporting-in-clinical-trials-regulatory-requirements-and-best-practices/.

results.title: Methodological quality in randomised clinical trials of mental health apps: systematic review and longitudinal analysis | BMJ Mental Health
results.content: The earliest reviews of trials of mental health apps highlighted several methodological issues, including the overuse of inactive/passive controls over active/placebo controls,5 6 the preponderance of trials with considerable risk of bias,7 8 high dropout rates coupled with inappropriate handling of missing data (complete case analyses),9 10 small sample sizes,7 lack of longer follow-ups11 and/or inadequate reporting of adverse events.11 These factors are widely known to reduce study quality and lead to an overestimation of the effects of psychological interventions.12–14 More recent syntheses of this field2 3 15–17 continue to emphasise these same methodological shortcomings, raising concerns about the empirical status of mental health apps.

results.title: Adverse Event Reporting in Early-Phase Benign Urology... : JU Open Plus
results.content: The purpose of this study was to compare serious adverse events (SAEs) and other study characteristics of benign vs malignant lower urinary tract clinical trials to understand safety and tolerability metrics as they apply to clinical trials of benign diseases. There are significantly higher rates of SAE, AE, and mortality in malignant bladder phase 1 trials, but no difference in therapy termination in comparison with benign trials. Trial characteristics included the number of subjects enrolled at baseline, the number of subjects receiving full therapy, academic vs nonacademic settings, location (single, multiple, or unspecified), US-based vs international, sponsorship (industry or investigator-initiated), result completion status (completed, terminated, or active but not recruiting), number of SAEs, number of AEs, whether AEs required therapy termination (yes, no, or missing), and all-cause mortality (none or yes). At the event level, for SAEs and AEs, respectively, the total count of the events, the average event per trial, and their SE were computed for all studies and further compared between benign and malignant studies using the _t_ tests. Interestingly, despite the differences in SAE and AE rates, there was no significant difference in the rate of AEs requiring therapy termination (4/18 benign trials vs 10/34 malignant trials, _P_ = .85). This study aims to highlight some key differences between malignant and benign lower urinary tract clinical trials, notably in the reporting of AEs and additional trial components. In this study, we demonstrated that there are significantly higher rates of SAE, AE, and mortality in malignant trials compared with benign trials. Limitations include incomplete reporting on ClinicalTrials.gov, possible subjectivity during trial screening, and lack of attribution information for AEs. Malignant trials were more likely to be conducted in academic centers and across multiple institutions, which could not only contribute to the findings but also highlight the need for more academic and multi-institutional benign studies. Specifically, more granular data such as AE details on severity and attribution, reasons for study dropout and therapy termination, and DLT definitions should be reported to strengthen clinical trial design and guide future therapeutic innovations in benign urology. This study demonstrated that there are significantly higher rates of SAE, AE, and mortality in malignant lower urinary tract phase 1 trials, but no difference in therapy termination in comparison with benign trials.
